glossario.simples: A way of organizing a country into parts that have their own governments but stay united.
Having its own tasks, laws and money.
The highest law of a municipality or of the Federal District. In Portuguese: lei orgânica.
Where the district deputies work. They make the laws of the Federal District. In Portuguese: Câmara Legislativa.
People elected to make the laws of the Federal District. In Portuguese: deputados distritais.
Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics), the agency that counts and studies Brazil's population and territory.
Instituto Nacional do Seguro Social (National Social Security Institute), the federal agency that pays retirement pensions and other benefits.
Money paid every month to people who worked and paid contributions for many years, for example when they reach a certain age.
A police force run by the Union. It also takes care of the borders and issues passports.
A document used to travel to other countries.
The Navy, the Army and the Air Force, which take care of the country's defense.
Sistema Único de Saúde (Unified Health System): free public health care all over Brazil.
The government of the city, headed by the mayor. In Portuguese: prefeitura.
A person elected to head the government of a state or of the Federal District.
The part of Brazil where Brasília is; it is neither a state nor a municipality. In Portuguese: Distrito Federal (DF).
The government of the whole of Brazil, also called the federal government. In Portuguese: União.
A city, with its neighborhoods and the countryside around it, and with its own government. In Portuguese: município.
Each of the 26 large parts of Brazil, with its own government.

slides.titulo: Brazil is like a three-story building
slides.texto: The floors are the Union (the whole country), the states and the municipalities (the cities). This is called a **federation**.

slides.titulo: Each floor has its own government
slides.texto: The three are **autonomous**: each one has its own tasks, its own laws and its own money.

cards.txt: It is the government of the whole of Brazil, also called the federal government.
cards.mais: The Constitution says that the union of the states, the municipalities and the Federal District cannot be undone. No state can break away from Brazil.

cards.txt: Each state has its own government and even its own Constitution.
cards.mais: Each state's Constitution must respect the Constitution of Brazil.

cards.txt: They are the cities, with their neighborhoods and the countryside around them.
cards.mais: The highest law of each municipality is called the organic law (lei orgânica). It is approved by the city councilors (vereadores).

slides.texto: See how many parts Brazil is divided into and how many people live here.
slides.nota: Numbers from the **IBGE**, Brazil's statistics institute. Municipalities: count from March 2026. People: estimate for July 1, 2026. Fernando de Noronha (an island in the state of Pernambuco) is not a municipality: it is a district of the state.

slides.titulo: What does the Union take care of?
slides.texto: The **Union** takes care of what applies to the whole of Brazil.

itens.txt: It makes the country's money: the bills and the coins.
It commands the Armed Forces: the Navy, the Army and the Air Force.
It talks and makes agreements with other countries.
It runs the Federal Police, which also issues passports.
It pays the retirement pensions of the INSS, the National Social Security Institute.

slides.coruja: Federal universities are also run by the Union.

slides.titulo: What does the state take care of?
slides.texto: The state government is headed by the **governor**.

itens.txt: The Military Police and the Civil Police (both are state police forces) and the Fire Department.
State schools, mostly high schools.
State hospitals, which are part of the SUS.
State prisons, which are guarded by the state's prison police.

slides.coruja: Elementary and middle school is shared: the state and the city take care of it together.

slides.titulo: What does the city take care of?
slides.texto: The **city government** (prefeitura) is headed by the mayor. It takes care of what is closest to you.

itens.txt: Daycare centers, preschools and elementary schools.
Health clinics.
Garbage collection and street cleaning.
The buses that run inside the city.
Streets, squares and streetlights.

slides.coruja: For many of these tasks, the city gets help from the state and the Union.

slides.texto: For each thing, choose: the country (Union), the state, the city or all together.

itens.txt: A pothole in the street where you live
itens.explica: Neighborhood streets belong to the municipality. The city government fixes them.

itens.txt: Military Police
itens.explica: The Military Police (PM), which patrols the streets, is under the command of the state governor.

itens.txt: A passport to travel
itens.explica: Passports are issued by the Federal Police, which is run by the Union.

itens.txt: The neighborhood health clinic
itens.explica: The city takes care of it, with help from the state and the Union.

itens.txt: Federal university
itens.explica: Federal universities are run by the Union.

itens.txt: Public high school
itens.explica: Public high schools are mainly the job of the states.

itens.txt: Garbage collection
itens.explica: Collecting the garbage from homes is a job of the municipality.

itens.txt: INSS retirement pension
itens.explica: The INSS is a federal agency: it pays the retirement pensions.

itens.txt: SUS, the public health system
itens.explica: The SUS is run by the Union, the states and the cities, together.

itens.txt: Protecting forests and animals
itens.explica: The Constitution gives this job to everyone: the Union, the states and the cities.

slides.texto: The **Federal District** (Distrito Federal, DF) is neither a state nor a municipality. It has a bit of both.

itens.txt: It cannot be divided into municipalities. That is why it has no mayor and no city councilors.
It is governed by the governor of the DF, who is elected together with the state governors.
The DF's laws are made by district deputies, in the Legislative Chamber (Câmara Legislativa).
The DF does the work of a state and of a city at the same time.
Brasília, the capital of Brazil, is in the DF.

slides.coruja: Fun fact: it is the Union that organizes and pays for the courts and the police of the DF.

slides.pergunta: If the street where you live has a pothole, who should fix it?
slides.explica: Neighborhood streets belong to the municipality, so the city government fixes them. Big roads (highways) may belong to the state or to the Union.

slides.pergunta: Does the Federal District have a mayor?
opcoes: No, because the DF cannot be divided into municipalities
slides.explica: The Constitution forbids dividing the DF into municipalities. The DF is governed by the governor of the DF.
